name: Space as a 'third nature'
plain_explanation: Besides the unchanging world of Ideas and the changing world of physical things, Plato proposes a strange third category -- space -- which is eternal like the Ideas but somehow provides a 'home' for changing physical things, and can barely be grasped by reason at all.
precise_definition: Timaeus's proposal of a third kind of being, alongside the unchanging intelligible essence and the changing sensible copy, namely an eternal, indestructible 'receptacle' or space, apprehended 'without the help of sense, by a kind of spurious reason,' which provides the necessary condition (a location) for anything sensible to exist at all.
why_it_mattered: Russell singles this out as 'a very difficult passage' arising from reflection on geometry (itself both purely rational, like arithmetic, and yet concerned with space, an aspect of the sensible world), and speculates that Kant, whose account of space also treats it as neither purely empirical nor purely intellectual, 'must have liked this view.'
examples: Space is described as apprehended 'as in a dream,' such that 'what is neither in heaven nor on earth has no existence.'
objections: Russell admits he does 'not pretend to understand [this passage] at all fully.'
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell speculatively connects it to Kant's treatment of space as a form of intuition, neither purely empirical nor purely conceptual.
